Mojtaba Khamenei is yet to be seen in public since succeeding his father. (Reuters: ISNA/WANA/Hamed Jafarnejad)

Not seen in public since he assumed the role in March, authorities are promising to release video of Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have increased attacks on Red Sea shipping, two days after Saudi Arabia signed a defence pact with Pakistan and Türkiye.

A deal with Oman defining new shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz is in its final stages but Iran has reiterated the strait will only reopen if the US met conditions.

Video footage of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since he assumed the role in March, has been promised by a paramilitary leader, according to Iranian state media.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei around the start of the president's third year in office in late July, but has given differing accounts in recent weeks about his access to Mr Khamenei.

On July 21, the president said interactions with the supreme leader were "increasing day by day", but in early August he said communicating with Khamenei was "very difficult".

Mr Khamenei was reportedly seriously injured in the February 28 strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

He had also generally kept a low public profile before becoming supreme leader.

Three sons of Iran's slain leader Ali Khamenei appear at his funeral in Tehran.  (ABC News)

The report on the Iranian judiciary's news outlet, Mizan, appeared to be aimed at quashing speculation about his health. Senior Iranian sources have said he suffered facial disfigurement.

Deputy Qasem Qoraishi from the Basij Organisation, a component of Iran's revolutionary guard, said on Sunday that footage would be released in the future.

Mr Qoraishi said the footage would "once again bring disgrace upon the enemies and detractors of the Iranian people".

The comments appeared to be aimed at countering speculation about Mr Khamenei's health and lack of public appearances.

On Sunday, local time, Iran said that a deal with Oman defining new shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz was in its final stages but reiterated that the strait would only reopen once the United States met other conditions.

A US official told Reuters on Friday that an agreement between Iran and Oman was close and could soon reopen the waterway, which carried a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before Iran blocked it in response to US and Israeli attacks.

Iran reiterated that the strait would only reopen once the United States met other conditions. (Reuters: Stringer)

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday, local time, that Iran and the US are not engaged in talks and Tehran will not start them as long as Washington breaches an interim deal signed in June, adding that messages are being exchanged via intermediaries.

Mr Araqchi repeated Iran's position that an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz between Tehran and Muscat was in the "final stages" but would not reopen the strategic waterway.

Iran and Oman are "very close" to reaching an accord on a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's foreign minister says. This is your three-minute briefing on the key developments overnight in the Middle East.

In comments reported by Mehr news agency, he said the agreement would set out the new shipping lanes to be used once the US fulfils other conditions and the strait is reopened to traffic.

Mr Trump would later tell US news outlet Axios the US was "only semi-negotiating" with Iran and was "low-keying it".

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," the US president said.

Iranian strikes on Strait of Hormuz shipping have been coupled with increased attacks by its Yemen-based allies, the Houthis.

In recent weeks, Houthis have targeted ships at another oil choke point on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

The Houthi rebels, described as one of Iran's "merchants of chaos", have threatened to widen the conflict in the Middle East by declaring a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. Here's what could happen next.

The Houthis also declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month in response to what they said was a Saudi siege on them in Yemen, an allegation denied by Riyadh, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The group said they had attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Sunday, two days after the kingdom signed a defence pact with Sunni Muslim allies Türkiye and Pakistan in response to growing regional instability from the US-Israeli war on Shiite Iran.

The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at the refinery but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the incident, without giving a cause.

The Houthis used a drone to target the refinery, military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on social media.

The group had struck Aramco sites before in Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day in south-western Saudi Arabia.

It was not clear whether or how either Pakistan or Türkiye would join in any Saudi response to the latest attack.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the new alliance was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support security.

The allies would decide through consultations what degree, form, and format of support they would ask for in the event of an attack, he said.
